Interpretation incorporating academic insights:
- Holding the target range at 4.25–4.5% while slowing the Treasury runoff cap from $25B to $5B is consistent with policy inertia/smoothing in New Keynesian estimates of optimal monetary policy (Clarida, Galí, and Gertler) and with a flexible-inflation-targeting, risk‑management approach emphasized by Svensson and Woodford. It keeps the stance restrictive against “somewhat elevated” inflation while modestly easing balance-sheet tightening.
- Maintaining IORB at 4.4% and using standing repo/reverse repo facilities reflects the modern floor-system operating framework discussed by Goodfriend (2002), allowing the Fed to control short rates precisely while separately calibrating balance-sheet policies.
- Slowing QT likely trims duration supply and term premium pressures, implying slightly easier financial conditions at the long end; this channel aligns with literature on term structure and policy’s influence on longer rates (e.g., Cochrane and Piazzesi). The Waller dissent favoring the prior, faster runoff underscores the internal debate over the marginal tightness of balance-sheet policy even with rates on hold.
Net tone: solid growth and a strong labor market with elevated inflation, but a small dovish tilt via reduced Treasury runoff under heightened uncertainty. Slightly more positive than before.
